chapters.title: Chapter 5: Risk Management for Trend and Momentum Strategies

lessons.title: Position Sizing for Trend and Momentum Portfolios

children.text: The last lesson showed how a single severe month can gut a strategy's average return even with a high win rate. Position sizing is the main lever that controls how much damage any single position, or any single tail event, can actually do. The same signal, sized two different ways, can produce a survivable strategy or an unsurvivable one.

body.text: Position sizing decides how much capital is at risk in each holding, independent of the ranking or trend signal itself. Equal capital in every position is the simplest approach, but it is not the same as equal risk, and the gap between the two matters a great deal for strategies with the fat-tailed, negatively skewed returns covered in the last lesson.

children.text: Chapter 4's case study used equal-weight sizing, the same rupee amount in every selected stock, for simplicity. Its real weakness is that it treats a calm, low-volatility large cap and a wild, high-volatility small cap as contributing equally to the portfolio, when in practice the volatile stock swings the portfolio's value far more per rupee invested. Equal capital is not equal risk.

body.caption: Inverse-volatility weighting: each position's weight is proportional to the reciprocal of its own volatility, so lower-volatility names receive larger weights and higher-volatility names receive smaller ones, equalizing each position's risk contribution rather than its capital contribution.

children.text: This is the standard approach used by most systematic trend-following and CTA funds, the same funds behind the crisis-alpha research from the last lesson. Reuse Chapter 4's risk-adjusted top 3, Q, R, and T, with volatilities of 22%, 18%, and 15% respectively.

body.caption: Equal-weight vs inverse-volatility weight on the same 3 stocks (from Chapter 4's worked example)

body.text: Q had the highest risk-adjusted momentum score of the three in Chapter 4, yet inverse-volatility sizing gives it the smallest position here, not the largest. Ranking and sizing answer two different questions: the ranking asks which stocks to hold, sizing asks how much of each, and conflating the two, giving the top-ranked name the biggest position by default, is a common mistake.

children.text: Beyond sizing individual positions relative to each other, many systematic funds also scale the entire portfolio's total exposure to hold its overall volatility near a fixed target, commonly called volatility targeting. When market-wide volatility rises, a portfolio's exposure is scaled down to keep total risk near target. When volatility falls, exposure is scaled up. This directly addresses the fat-tail problem from the last lesson: rather than accepting whatever risk level the market happens to hand the portfolio in a given month, the portfolio actively manages toward a consistent risk level over time, though it cannot eliminate a sudden, single-day shock that arrives faster than the exposure can be adjusted.
The Kelly Criterion, and Why Practitioners Use a Fraction of It

body.caption: The Kelly criterion: the theoretically optimal fraction of capital to risk per bet, where p is the probability of winning, q = 1 - p is the probability of losing, and b is the ratio of a typical win's size to a typical loss's size.

children.text: The Kelly criterion calculates the position size that maximizes long-run compound growth given a known edge. In practice, almost no one sizes at full Kelly. The formula assumes you know your true win probability and payoff ratio exactly, when in reality both are estimated from limited historical data with real uncertainty, and full Kelly sizing produces extremely large drawdowns even when the edge is real, exactly the fat-tail risk from the last lesson. Most practitioners size at a fraction of full Kelly, commonly half or less, deliberately trading away some theoretical long-run growth for a survivable ride along the way.

body.caption: Inverse-volatility position sizing
body.code:
import pandas as pd

selected = pd.DataFrame({
    "volatility": [0.22, 0.18, 0.15],
}, index=["Q", "R", "T"])

inverse_vol = 1 / selected["volatility"]
selected["weight"] = inverse_vol / inverse_vol.sum()

print(selected)

body.title: A two-stock inverse-volatility calculation
body.prompt: Stock X has 20% volatility, Stock Y has 40% volatility. Using inverse-volatility weighting between just these two stocks, what weight, in percent, does Stock X receive?
body.explanation: (1/20) / ((1/20) + (1/40)) = 0.05 / 0.075 = 0.6667, or 66.67%. Stock X's volatility is half of Stock Y's, so it receives exactly twice Stock Y's weight, 66.67% versus 33.33%.

body.title: Ranking vs sizing
body.question: A momentum ranking system's top-scoring stock has the highest volatility among the selected names. Under inverse-volatility position sizing, what happens to this stock's allocation?
options: It automatically receives the largest position, since it ranked first
It is excluded from the portfolio entirely, since high volatility disqualifies it
It likely receives a smaller position than lower-volatility names, since sizing is based on volatility, not rank
Its position size doubles automatically to compensate for the extra risk
body.explanation: Inverse-volatility sizing is based purely on each stock's own volatility, not its rank. A high-volatility name, even if it ranked first, typically receives a smaller position than a lower-volatility name under this scheme.

body.title: Why not size at full Kelly?
body.scenario: A trader calculates their momentum strategy's historical win rate and average win/loss ratio, plugs them into the Kelly formula, and gets a recommended position size of 45% of capital per trade. A friend suggests using 15% instead.
body.prompt: Based on this lesson, why might the friend's suggestion be more sensible than sizing at the full Kelly-recommended level?
body.modelAnswer: The Kelly formula assumes the win probability and payoff ratio used are exactly correct, but both are only estimates from limited historical data and carry real uncertainty. Sizing at the full Kelly-recommended level also produces very large drawdowns even when the underlying edge is genuine, which is especially dangerous for a strategy already prone to the fat tails and negative skew covered in the last lesson. Using a fraction of full Kelly, such as the friend's 15% against a calculated 45%, deliberately gives up some theoretical long-run growth in exchange for a much more survivable ride, a standard practitioner adjustment for real-world estimation error.

cards.definition: A position sizing method that weights each holding proportional to the reciprocal of its own volatility, equalizing risk contribution rather than capital contribution.
Scaling a portfolio's total exposure up or down over time to keep its overall realized volatility near a fixed target level.
A formula for the theoretically optimal fraction of capital to risk per bet, given a known win probability and payoff ratio, to maximize long-run compound growth.
Sizing positions at a fraction, commonly half or less, of the full Kelly-recommended size, to account for estimation error and reduce drawdown severity.

points: Equal-weight sizing gives equal capital to every position, but not equal risk, since more volatile stocks swing a portfolio's value more per rupee invested.

Inverse-volatility weighting sizes each position based on its own volatility, equalizing risk contribution, and can give a top-ranked but volatile stock a smaller position than a lower-ranked but calmer one.
Volatility targeting scales an entire portfolio's exposure over time to keep overall risk near a consistent level, though it cannot fully protect against a sudden, single-day shock.

The Kelly criterion gives a theoretically optimal position size, but almost no practitioner uses full Kelly, since real-world estimation error and fat-tail risk make a fractional Kelly approach far more survivable.
Position sizing and signal generation are two separate decisions. Conflating them, by default giving the top-ranked or most convincing signal the largest position, is a common and avoidable mistake.
